claim: The Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes enabled the discovery of sequences that differ between modern and archaic humans, the majority of which are noncoding.
source: The Neanderthal and Denisovan genomes enabled the discovery of sequences that differ between modern and archaic humans, the majority of which are noncoding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the genomes and is supported by the existence of these sequenced genomes.

claim: 14,042 single-nucleotide modern human-specific variants were investigated using massively parallel reporter assay.
source: Here, we used a massively parallel reporter assay in embryonic stem cells, neural progenitor cells, and bone osteoblasts to investigate the regulatory effects of the 14,042 single-nucleotide modern human-specific variants.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental design and the number of variants tested.

claim: 1791 (13%) of sequences containing modern human-specific variants showed active regulatory activity.
source: Overall, 1791 (13%) of sequences containing these variants showed active regulatory activity, and 407 (23%) of these drove differential expression between human groups.
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA experiment reported in the abstract and results sections.

claim: 407 (23%) of active sequences drove differential expression between modern and archaic human groups.
source: Overall, 1791 (13%) of sequences containing these variants showed active regulatory activity, and 407 (23%) of these drove differential expression between human groups.
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA experiment reported in the abstract.

claim: Differentially active sequences were associated with divergent transcription factor binding motifs.
source: Differentially active sequences were associated with divergent transcription factor binding motifs, and with genes enriched for vocal tract and brain anatomy and function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational analysis of TF binding motifs in the results section.

claim: Differentially active sequences were associated with genes enriched for vocal tract and brain anatomy and function.
source: Differentially active sequences were associated with divergent transcription factor binding motifs, and with genes enriched for vocal tract and brain anatomy and function.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by Gene ORGANizer and HPO enrichment analyses in the results section.

claim: Modern human faces are flat with smaller jaws compared to archaic humans.
source: For example, our face is flat with smaller jaws, our development is slower, our pelvises are narrower, our limbs tend to be slenderer, and our brain differs in its substructure proportions (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002) (especially the cerebellum; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenotypic difference and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Modern human development is slower compared to archaic humans.
source: For example, our face is flat with smaller jaws, our development is slower, our pelvises are narrower, our limbs tend to be slenderer, and our brain differs in its substructure proportions (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002) (especially the cerebellum; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenotypic difference and supported by citations.

claim: Modern human pelvises are narrower compared to archaic humans.
source: For example, our face is flat with smaller jaws, our development is slower, our pelvises are narrower, our limbs tend to be slenderer, and our brain differs in its substructure proportions (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002) (especially the cerebellum; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenotypic difference and supported by citations.

claim: Modern human limbs tend to be slenderer compared to archaic humans.
source: For example, our face is flat with smaller jaws, our development is slower, our pelvises are narrower, our limbs tend to be slenderer, and our brain differs in its substructure proportions (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002) (especially the cerebellum; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenotypic difference and supported by citations.

claim: Modern human brains differ in substructure proportions compared to archaic humans, especially the cerebellum.
source: For example, our face is flat with smaller jaws, our development is slower, our pelvises are narrower, our limbs tend to be slenderer, and our brain differs in its substructure proportions (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002) (especially the cerebellum; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known phenotypic difference and supported by citations, with specific emphasis on the cerebellum.

claim: The vast majority of genetic changes that separate modern and archaic humans are found outside protein-coding regions.
source: The vast majority of genetic changes that separate modern and archaic humans are found outside protein-coding regions, and some of these likely affect gene expression (Yan and McCoy, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Some noncoding genetic changes between modern and archaic humans likely affect gene expression.
source: The vast majority of genetic changes that separate modern and archaic humans are found outside protein-coding regions, and some of these likely affect gene expression (Yan and McCoy, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation.

claim: Alterations in gene regulation are thought to underlie most of the phenotypic differences between closely related groups.
source: Such regulatory changes may have a sizeable impact on human evolution, as alterations in gene regulation are thought to underlie most of the phenotypic differences between closely related groups (Britten and Davidson, 1971; King and Wilson, 1975; Enard et al., 2014; Fraser, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in evolutionary biology and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Many noncoding variants that emerged in modern humans have altered gene expression in cis.
source: Indeed, there is mounting evidence that many of the noncoding variants that emerged in modern humans have altered gene expression in cis, shaped phenotypes, and have been under selection (Yan and McCoy, 2020; McCoy et al., 2017; Petr et al., 2019; Gokhman et al., 2020; Colbran, 2019; Gokhman et al., 2019; Dannemann and Racimo, 2018; Weyer and Pääbo, 2016; Vespasiani et al., 2020; Grogan and Perry, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: RNA molecules and epigenetic marks are absent in degraded archaic human samples.
source: In archaic humans, incomplete information on gene regulation is further exacerbated by the lack of RNA molecules and epigenetic marks in these degraded samples (Yan and McCoy, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of studying archaic samples and supported by a citation.

claim: Whole-genome archaic DNA methylation maps have been reconstructed using patterns of cytosine degradation in ancient samples.
source: We have previously used patterns of cytosine degradation in ancient samples to reconstruct whole-genome archaic DNA methylation maps (Gokhman et al., 2020; Gokhman et al., 2014; Gokhman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as previous work by the authors and supported by citations to their own publications.

claim: Understanding of gene regulation in archaic humans remains minimal.
source: However, despite various approaches to extract regulatory information from ancient genomes (Yan and McCoy, 2020; Colbran, 2019; Gokhman et al., 2016; Barker et al., 2020; Batyrev et al., 2019; Pedersen et al., 2014; Silvert et al., 2019; Moriano and Boeckx, 2020), our understanding of gene regulation in archaic humans remains minimal, with most archaic regulatory information being currently inaccessible (Yan and McCoy, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field and supported by citations.

claim: eQTL mapping can only be applied to loci that are variable within the present-day human population.
source: Additionally, whereas expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) mapping can be used to identify variants that drive differential expression between individuals, it can only be applied to loci that are variable within the present-day human population.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of eQTL mapping methodology.

claim: Fixed noncoding variants are particularly difficult to characterize.
source: Therefore, fixed noncoding variants are of particular interest in the study of human evolution, but are also particularly difficult to characterize.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field that motivates the current study.

claim: MPRA provides the ability to interrogate the regulatory effects of thousands of variants en masse.
source: Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) provide the ability to interrogate the regulatory effects of thousands of variants en masse (Inoue and Ahituv, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the MPRA method and supported by a citation.

claim: MPRA is an effective high-throughput tool to identify variants underlying divergent regulation in organisms where experimental options are limited.
source: Thus, MPRA is an effective high-throughput tool to identify variants underlying divergent regulation, especially in organisms where experimental options are limited (Tewhey et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2018; Ryu et al., 2018; Uebbing et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of MPRA and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The study used three Neanderthal genomes, one Denisovan genome, and 114 chimpanzee, bonobo, and gorilla genomes to define modern human-specific variants.
source: To define a set of variants that likely emerged and reached fixation or near fixation along the modern human lineage, we took all the single-nucleotide variants where modern humans differ from archaic humans and great apes (based on three Neanderthal genomes [Prüfer et al., 2014; Prüfer et al., 2017; Mafessoni et al., 2020], one Denisovan genome [Meyer et al., 2012], and 114 chimpanzee, bonobo, and gorilla genomes [de Manuel et al., 2016]).
evidence: This describes the data sources used in the study with specific citations.

claim: Polymorphic sites within modern humans were excluded from the variant set.
source: We excluded any polymorphic sites within modern humans (in either the 1000 Genomes Project [Auton et al., 2015] or in dbSNP [Sherry et al., 2001]), or within archaic humans and great apes (Prüfer et al., 2014; Prüfer et al., 2017; Mafessoni et al., 2020; Meyer et al., 2012; de Manuel et al., 2016) (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the filtering criteria used to select variants.

claim: The resulting set of 14,042 variants comprises changes that likely emerged and reached fixation or near fixation along the modern human lineage.
source: The resulting set of 14,042 variants comprises those changes that likely emerged and reached fixation or near fixation along the modern human lineage (Supplementary file 1a-c).
evidence: This is the final set of variants analyzed in the study after applying all filters.

claim: The vast majority of the 14,042 variants are intergenic.
source: The vast majority of these variants are intergenic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a figure showing the genomic distribution of variants.

claim: The variant list does not include variants that introgressed from archaic humans into modern humans.
source: By definition, this list does not include variants that introgressed from archaic humans into modern humans and spread to detectable frequencies.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the filtering criteria used.

claim: 97% of sequences had at least 10 barcodes associated with them.
source: 97% of sequences had at least 10 barcodes associated with them, with a median of 96 barcodes per sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: This describes the barcode coverage achieved in the MPRA experiment.

claim: Chromosomally integrating constructs show improved technical reproducibility compared to episomal constructs.
source: Furthermore, we used a chromosomally integrating construct rather than an episomal construct due to the improved technical reproducibility and correlation of results from chromosomally integrating constructs with functional genomic signals like TF ChIP-seq and histone acetylation marks (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for the experimental design and supported by a citation.

claim: MPRAs generally replicate the endogenous activity of sequences.
source: Importantly, despite the caveat of interrogating sequences outside of their endogenous context, MPRAs were shown to generally replicate the endogenous activity of sequences (Inoue et al., 2017; Klein et al., 2020; Kircher et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the MPRA approach and supported by citations.

claim: The brain and skeleton have been the focus of evolutionary studies due to their extensive phenotypic divergence among human lineages.
source: The brain and skeleton have been the focus of evolutionary studies due to their extensive phenotypic divergence among human lineages (Aiello and Dean, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for cell type selection and supported by a citation.

claim: Strong correlation of RNA/DNA ratios was observed between replicates for all cell types (Pearson's r = 0.76–0.96, p<10−100).
source: We saw a strong correlation of RNA/DNA ratios between replicates for all cell types (Pearson's r = 0.76–0.96, p<10−100, Figure 1—figure supplement 2b), with the lower correlation scores being in ESC, likely due to our use of lower multiplicity of infection (MOI) in these cells due to their increased sensitivity to lentivirus infection.
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA experiment showing technical reproducibility.

claim: The mean RNA/DNA ratio of scrambled sequences was lower than that of positive control sequences in ESCs (p=2.7×10−8) and NPCs (p=1.8×10−6).
source: The mean RNA/DNA ratio of the scrambled sequences was lower than that of the positive control sequences in ESCs and NPCs (p=2.7×10−8 for ESCs and p=1.8×10−6 for NPCs, t-test, see 'Materials and methods', Figure 1—figure supplement 2d), but not in osteoblasts (p=0.25).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of control sequences showing the assay can distinguish active from inactive sequences.

claim: In ESCs, 8% (1183) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles.
source: We found that in ESCs, 8% (1183) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles, 6% (814) in osteoblasts, and 4% (602) in NPCs (FDR <0.05, Supplementary file 1a-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA analysis identifying active sequences.

claim: In osteoblasts, 6% (814) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles.
source: We found that in ESCs, 8% (1183) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles, 6% (814) in osteoblasts, and 4% (602) in NPCs (FDR <0.05, Supplementary file 1a-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA analysis identifying active sequences.

claim: In NPCs, 4% (602) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles.
source: We found that in ESCs, 8% (1183) of sequence pairs drove expression in at least one of the alleles, 6% (814) in osteoblasts, and 4% (602) in NPCs (FDR <0.05, Supplementary file 1a-c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2d, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA analysis identifying active sequences.

claim: 13% (1791) of archaic and modern human sequence pairs were active in at least one cell type.
source: Overall, 13% (1791) of archaic and modern human sequence pairs were active in at least one cell type, 4% (586) in at least two cell types, and 2% (222) in all three cell types (overlap of 75-fold higher than expected, p<10−100, Super Exact test; Wang et al., 2015, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a summary result combining data across all three cell types.

claim: 4% (586) of sequence pairs were active in at least two cell types.
source: Overall, 13% (1791) of archaic and modern human sequence pairs were active in at least one cell type, 4% (586) in at least two cell types, and 2% (222) in all three cell types (overlap of 75-fold higher than expected, p<10−100, Super Exact test; Wang et al., 2015, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a summary result showing overlap of active sequences across cell types.

claim: 2% (222) of sequence pairs were active in all three cell types.
source: Overall, 13% (1791) of archaic and modern human sequence pairs were active in at least one cell type, 4% (586) in at least two cell types, and 2% (222) in all three cell types (overlap of 75-fold higher than expected, p<10−100, Super Exact test; Wang et al., 2015, Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a summary result showing overlap of active sequences across all cell types.

claim: Active sequences were 1.6- to 2.7-fold more likely than inactive sequences to have active chromatin marks, depending on cell type.
source: We found that on average, active sequences were 1.6- to 2.7-fold more likely than inactive sequences to have active chromatin marks, depending on cell type.
evidence: This is a result from comparing active sequences to chromatin mark data.

claim: Active sequences are enriched for promoter and enhancer marks compared to inactive sequences.
source: Compared to inactive sequences, we found that active sequences are enriched for promoter and enhancer marks (FDR <0.05 in each of the cell types for overlap with active TSS and enhancers, Figure 2e, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1f, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from chromHMM annotation analysis showing functional characteristics of active sequences.

claim: Active sequences are 6–32% closer to GTEx eQTLs compared to inactive sequences, depending on cell type.
source: We also found that compared to inactive sequences, active sequences are 6–32% closer to GTEx (GTEx Consortium, 2015) eQTLs, depending on cell type (FDR <0.05, t-test).
evidence: This is a result from comparing active sequences to eQTL locations.

claim: Active sequences are 1.2–1.3× closer to transcription start sites compared to inactive sequences.
source: Active sequences are also 1.2–1.3× closer to transcription start sites (TSS), with 32–39% of them located within 10 kb of a TSS, depending on cell type (FDR <0.05, t-test, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from comparing active sequences to TSS locations.

claim: Active sequences are significantly hypomethylated compared to inactive sequences in osteoblasts (p=5.5×10−13).
source: We found that active sequences are significantly hypomethylated compared to inactive sequences (p=5.5×10−13, t-test, Figure 2f) and that their activity level (RNA/DNA ratio) is negatively correlated with methylation levels (6.0 × 10−9, Pearson's r = −0.24).
evidence: This is a result from comparing active sequences to DNA methylation data.

claim: Active sequence activity level (RNA/DNA ratio) is negatively correlated with methylation levels (p=6.0×10−9, Pearson's r = −0.24).
source: We found that active sequences are significantly hypomethylated compared to inactive sequences (p=5.5×10−13, t-test, Figure 2f) and that their activity level (RNA/DNA ratio) is negatively correlated with methylation levels (6.0 × 10−9, Pearson's r = −0.24).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result showing relationship between activity and methylation.

claim: Active sequences show slightly higher sequence conservation in primates compared to inactive sequences (PhyloP: −0.05 for inactive, −0.04 for active, FDR = 1.1×10−3).
source: Finally, compared to inactive sequences, active sequences show slightly higher sequence conservation in primates, indicating a potential functional role (PhyloP, −0.05 on average for inactive, −0.04 for active, FDR = 1.1×10−3, t-test) with more highly active sequences showing higher conservation levels (e.g., 0.24 for active sequences with RNA/DNA ratio ≥4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from comparing active sequences to sequence conservation scores.

claim: Out of active sequence pairs in ESCs, 110 (9%) drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans.
source: Out of the active sequence pairs in each cell type, 110 (9%) in ESCs drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans, 243 (30%) in osteoblasts, and 153 (25%) in NPCs (FDR ≤ 0.05, see Materials and methods, Figure 3a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Discussion for cell-type differences).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Out of active sequence pairs in osteoblasts, 243 (30%) drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans.
source: Out of the active sequence pairs in each cell type, 110 (9%) in ESCs drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans, 243 (30%) in osteoblasts, and 153 (25%) in NPCs (FDR ≤ 0.05, see Materials and methods, Figure 3a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Discussion for cell-type differences).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: Out of active sequence pairs in NPCs, 153 (25%) drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans.
source: Out of the active sequence pairs in each cell type, 110 (9%) in ESCs drive significantly differential expression between modern and archaic humans, 243 (30%) in osteoblasts, and 153 (25%) in NPCs (FDR ≤ 0.05, see Materials and methods, Figure 3a–c, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, see Discussion for cell-type differences).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis.

claim: 407 sequences (23% of active sequences) were differentially active in at least one cell type.
source: Overall, we see significant overlap between cell types in differentially active sequences: 407 sequences (23% of active sequences) were differentially active in at least one cell type, 89 (5%) in at least two cell types, and 10 (0.6%) in all three cell types (eightfold higher than expected compared to active sequences, p=5×10−7, Super Exact test (Wang et al., 2015), Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a summary result combining differentially active sequences across cell types.

claim: 89 (5%) sequences were differentially active in at least two cell types.
source: Overall, we see significant overlap between cell types in differentially active sequences: 407 sequences (23% of active sequences) were differentially active in at least one cell type, 89 (5%) in at least two cell types, and 10 (0.6%) in all three cell types (eightfold higher than expected compared to active sequences, p=5×10−7, Super Exact test (Wang et al., 2015), Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a summary result showing overlap of differentially active sequences across cell types.

claim: 10 (0.6%) sequences were differentially active in all three cell types.
source: Overall, we see significant overlap between cell types in differentially active sequences: 407 sequences (23% of active sequences) were differentially active in at least one cell type, 89 (5%) in at least two cell types, and 10 (0.6%) in all three cell types (eightfold higher than expected compared to active sequences, p=5×10−7, Super Exact test (Wang et al., 2015), Figure 3d).
evidence: This is a summary result showing overlap of differentially active sequences across all cell types.

claim: Of the 407 differentially active sequences, the median fold-change was 1.2×.
source: As expected from such closely related organisms, and similar to other MPRAs that compared nucleotide variants (see Discussion), including one that compared human and chimp sequences (Ryu et al., 2018), most sequences drove modest magnitudes of expression difference; of the 407 differentially active sequences, the median fold-change was 1.2×, and only five sequences had a fold-change greater than 2× (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a summary statistic of the magnitude of differential expression observed.

claim: Only five differentially active sequences had a fold-change greater than 2×.
source: As expected from such closely related organisms, and similar to other MPRAs that compared nucleotide variants (see Discussion), including one that compared human and chimp sequences (Ryu et al., 2018), most sequences drove modest magnitudes of expression difference; of the 407 differentially active sequences, the median fold-change was 1.2×, and only five sequences had a fold-change greater than 2× (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: This is a summary statistic of the magnitude of differential expression observed.

claim: In ESCs and NPCs, sequences were equally likely to be up- or downregulating (51% and 52% of differentially active sequences were downregulating).
source: In ESCs and NPCs, sequences were equally likely to be up- or downregulating (51% and 52% of differentially active sequences were downregulating, p=0.92 and 0.63, respectively, binomial test), while in osteoblasts downregulation was observed slightly more often (59%, p=6.9×10−3).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the directionality of differential expression.

claim: In osteoblasts, downregulation was observed slightly more often (59%, p=6.9×10−3).
source: In ESCs and NPCs, sequences were equally likely to be up- or downregulating (51% and 52% of differentially active sequences were downregulating, p=0.92 and 0.63, respectively, binomial test), while in osteoblasts downregulation was observed slightly more often (59%, p=6.9×10−3).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the directionality of differential expression.

claim: 87 out of 89 sequence pairs that are differentially active in two cell types show agreement in the direction of differential activity (p=6.5×10−24).
source: We found a strong agreement in the direction of differential activity across cell types (87 out of 89 of sequence pairs that are differentially active in two cell types, p=6.5×10−24, and 10 out of 10 for three cell types, p=9.5×10−7, binomial test).
evidence: This is a result showing consistency of differential activity direction across cell types.

claim: 10 out of 10 sequence pairs that are differentially active in all three cell types show agreement in the direction of differential activity (p=9.5×10−7).
source: We found a strong agreement in the direction of differential activity across cell types (87 out of 89 of sequence pairs that are differentially active in two cell types, p=6.5×10−24, and 10 out of 10 for three cell types, p=9.5×10−7, binomial test).
evidence: This is a result showing consistency of differential activity direction across all cell types.

claim: High correlation was observed between the magnitudes of differential activity across cell types (Pearson's r = 0.82, p=1.6×10−27).
source: We also observed a high correlation between the magnitudes of differential activity (Pearson's r = 0.82, p=1.6×10−27).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result showing consistency of effect sizes across cell types.

claim: The direction of expression change is identical in all pairs of overlapping sequences (p=2.0×10−3).
source: We found that the direction of expression change is identical in all pairs of overlapping sequences (p=2.0×10−3, binomial test), and that the magnitude of their expression change is highly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.95, 2.4 × 10−5, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a validation result showing consistency between overlapping sequences.

claim: The magnitude of expression change in overlapping sequences is highly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.95, p=2.4×10−5).
source: We found that the direction of expression change is identical in all pairs of overlapping sequences (p=2.0×10−3, binomial test), and that the magnitude of their expression change is highly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.95, 2.4 × 10−5, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a validation result showing consistency between overlapping sequences.

claim: 9 out of 12 sequences tested in luciferase assay replicated the lentiMPRA results in direction and magnitude (Pearson's r = 0.67, p=3.7×10−4).
source: To validate these results with an orthogonal method, we tested four differentially active sequences from each cell type in a luciferase reporter assay and found that the direction and magnitude of differential expression tended to replicate the lentiMPRA results (9 out of 12 sequences, Pearson's r = 0.67, p=3.7×10−4, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c, Supplementary file 1g).
evidence: This is a validation result using an orthogonal experimental method.

claim: Between 33% and 45% of differentially active sequences are within 10 kb of a TSS, depending on cell type.
source: Finally, we examined the endogenous genomic locations of differentially active sequences, focusing on promoters and enhancers. Between 33% and 45% of these sequences are within 10 kb of a TSS (depending on cell type, Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the genomic locations of differentially active sequences.

claim: Between 20% and 25% of differentially active sequences are within putative promoter or enhancer regions.
source: Analyzing chromHMM (Ernst and Kellis, 2012; Kundaje et al., 2015), we found that between 20% and 25% of the differentially active sequences are within putative promoter or enhancer regions (Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a result from chromHMM annotation analysis.

claim: Differentially active sequences are over-represented within putative enhancer regions in NPCs (2.2-fold, FDR = 0.03).
source: We found that differentially active sequences are over-represented within putative enhancer regions in NPCs (2.2-fold, FDR = 0.03, Fisher's exact test, Figure 1—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is a result from enrichment analysis comparing differentially active to other active sequences.

claim: Upregulating sequences have a tendency to be hypomethylated in modern compared to archaic humans (on average −2% methylation).
source: We found that upregulating sequences indeed have a slight but significant tendency to be hypomethylated in modern compared to archaic humans, and that downregulating sequences tend to be hypermethylated in modern compared to archaic humans (on average −2% methylation in upregulating sequences and +1% methylation in downregulating sequences in the modern compared to the archaic genomes, p=0.028, paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from comparing methylation levels between modern and archaic sequences.

claim: Downregulating sequences tend to be hypermethylated in modern compared to archaic humans (on average +1% methylation).
source: We found that upregulating sequences indeed have a slight but significant tendency to be hypomethylated in modern compared to archaic humans, and that downregulating sequences tend to be hypermethylated in modern compared to archaic humans (on average −2% methylation in upregulating sequences and +1% methylation in downregulating sequences in the modern compared to the archaic genomes, p=0.028, paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is a result from comparing methylation levels between modern and archaic sequences.

claim: Upregulating promoter sequences have +5% methylation on average in modern compared to archaic genomes, while downregulating promoter sequences have −8% methylation (p=0.034).
source: Indeed, we found that upregulating promoter sequences have +5% methylation on average in the modern compared to the archaic genomes, while downregulating promoter sequences have −8% methylation (p=0.034, paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing methylation in promoter regions specifically.

claim: In CpG-poor promoters, upregulating sequences show −15% methylation and downregulating sequences show +15% methylation in modern compared to archaic humans (p=6×10−3).
source: This trend is more pronounced in CpG-poor promoters, where the link between methylation and expression is known to be stronger (Lister et al., 2009; Stadler et al., 2011; Schlesinger et al., 2013) (−15% methylation in upregulating sequences and +15% methylation in downregulating promoter sequences in modern compared to archaic humans; p=6×10−3, paired t-test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing methylation in CpG-poor promoter regions specifically.

claim: The difference in predicted TF binding between modern and archaic alleles is larger for differentially active sequences compared to other active sequences (4.3×, p=0.02).
source: We found that (1) compared to other active sequences, the difference in predicted binding between the modern and archaic human alleles tends to be larger for differentially active sequences (combined across cell types: 4.3×, p=0.02, t-test, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d);
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis of TF binding motifs.

claim: The directionality of differential expression tends to match the directionality of differential TF binding (p=3.7×10−6 for ESCs, p=1.7×10−6 for osteoblasts, and p=1.3×10−5 for NPCs).
source: (2) the directionality of differential expression tends to match the directionality of differential binding, that is, upregulating sequences tend to have stronger predicted binding for the modern human sequence, whereas downregulating sequences tend to have stronger predicted binding for the archaic sequence (p=3.7×10−6 for ESCs, p=1.7×10−6 for osteoblasts, and p=1.3×10−5 for NPCs, binomial test, Figure 3e, see Materials and methods);
evidence: This is a result from comparing predicted TF binding to observed expression changes.

claim: The magnitude of expression difference is correlated with the magnitude of predicted TF binding difference (Pearson's r = 0.43, p=1.2×10−3 for ESCs; r = 0.23, p=0.02 for osteoblasts; r = 0.35, p=2.4×10−3 for NPCs).
source: and (3) the magnitude of expression difference is correlated with the magnitude of predicted binding difference (Pearson's r = 0.43 and p=1.2×10−3 for ESCs, Pearson's r = 0.23 and p=0.02 for osteoblasts, and Pearson's r = 0.35 and p=2.4×10−3 for NPCs, Figure 3—figure supplement 2a–c and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a correlation analysis result linking predicted TF binding to expression changes.

claim: Changes to the motifs of 14 TFs were predictive of expression changes.
source: We found that changes to the motifs of 14 TFs were predictive of expression changes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2d, Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing which TF motif changes correlate with expression changes.

claim: ZNF281 is significantly enriched in differentially active sequences in NPCs (14 out of 153 sequences, 4.6-fold, FDR = 0.04).
source: We found that ZNF281, an inhibitor of neuronal differentiation (Pieraccioli et al., 2018), is significantly enriched: out of 153 differentially active sequences in NPCs, 14 are predicted to be bound by ZNF281 (4.6-fold, FDR = 0.04, Supplementary file 3c).
evidence: This is a result from motif enrichment analysis in differentially active sequences.

claim: ZNF281 is an inhibitor of neuronal differentiation.
source: We found that ZNF281, an inhibitor of neuronal differentiation (Pieraccioli et al., 2018), is significantly enriched: out of 153 differentially active sequences in NPCs, 14 are predicted to be bound by ZNF281 (4.6-fold, FDR = 0.04, Supplementary file 3c).
evidence: This is stated as a known function of ZNF281 and supported by a citation.

claim: 1341 (75%) out of the 1791 active sequences were linked to at least one putative target gene.
source: Overall, 1341 (75%) out of the 1791 active sequences were linked to at least one putative target gene (Supplementary file 1h).
evidence: This is a result from linking sequences to genes using multiple data sources.

claim: Genes linked to downregulating sequences are enriched for vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts).
source: First, we tested Gene Ontology terms and found an enrichment of the following terms within downregulating sequences: vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts), regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs), and protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes linked to downregulating sequences are enriched for regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs).
source: First, we tested Gene Ontology terms and found an enrichment of the following terms within downregulating sequences: vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts), regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs), and protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes linked to downregulating sequences are enriched for protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs).
source: First, we tested Gene Ontology terms and found an enrichment of the following terms within downregulating sequences: vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts), regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs), and protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes linked to downregulating sequences are enriched for multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs).
source: First, we tested Gene Ontology terms and found an enrichment of the following terms within downregulating sequences: vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts), regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs), and protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: Genes linked to downregulating sequences are enriched for protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts).
source: First, we tested Gene Ontology terms and found an enrichment of the following terms within downregulating sequences: vesicle-mediated transport (6.6-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in osteoblasts), regulation of apoptotic process (6.0-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), protein ubiquitination (4.7-fold, FDR = 1.9×10−3, in ESCs), multicellular organism development (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.01, in ESCs), and protein transport (3.3-fold, FDR = 0.02, in osteoblasts, Figure 3—figure supplement 2f, Supplementary file 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: For genes linked to upregulating sequences, the most enriched body parts belong to the vocal tract: vocal cords (5.0-fold, FDR = 1.3×10−3), voice box/larynx (3.8-fold, FDR = 4.8×10−3), and pharynx (3.3-fold, FDR = 9.5×10−3), all within ESCs.
source: We analyzed the genes linked to differentially active sequences and found that for genes linked to sequences driving upregulation, the most enriched body parts belong to the vocal tract, that is, the vocal cords (5.0-fold, FDR = 1.3×10−3), voice box (larynx, 3.8-fold, FDR = 4.8×10−3), and pharynx (3.3-fold, FDR = 9.5×10−3, all within ESCs, Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a result from Gene ORGANizer enrichment analysis.

claim: The most extensive DNA methylation changes in modern compared to archaic humans arose in genes affecting the vocal cords and voice box.
source: Interestingly, we have previously reported that the most extensive DNA methylation changes in modern compared to archaic humans arose in genes affecting the vocal cords and voice box (Gokhman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as a previous finding by the authors and supported by a citation.

claim: Within sequences driving downregulation, the enriched body part is the cerebellum (3.0-fold, FDR = 9.2×10−3, in NPCs).
source: Conversely, within sequences driving downregulation, the enriched body part is the cerebellum (3.0-fold, FDR = 9.2×10−3, in NPCs, Figure 4a, Supplementary file 4b).
evidence: This is a result from Gene ORGANizer enrichment analysis.

claim: The biggest differences in brain anatomy between modern humans and Neanderthals are in the cerebellum.
source: This is in line with previous reports of cerebellar anatomy differences between modern humans and Neanderthals (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002), including results suggesting that the biggest differences in brain anatomy are in the cerebellum (Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a known finding from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: The differentially active sequence in SATB2 is found at a position that is relatively conserved in vertebrates (PhyloP score = 0.996).
source: First, we analyzed its linked variant (C to T transition), which is at a position that is relatively conserved in vertebrates (GRCh38: 199,469,203 on chromosome 2, PhyloP score = 0.996).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the conservation of the variant position.

claim: The SATB2 variant position is found within a CpG island between two alternative TSS of SATB2.
source: This position is found within a CpG island between two alternative TSS of SATB2 (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the genomic context of the variant.

claim: The SATB2 variant is found in the first intron of SATB2-AS1, an antisense lncRNA which upregulates SATB2 protein levels.
source: It is also found in the first intron of SATB2-AS1, an antisense lncRNA which upregulates SATB2 protein levels (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a genomic location and function of SATB2-AS1, supported by a citation.

claim: The SATB2 variant position overlaps a DNase I-hypersensitive site.
source: We found that it overlaps a DNase I-hypersensitive site (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) and shows many peaks of active histone modification marks in all three cell types (Figure 4c, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing chromatin accessibility data.

claim: The SATB2 sequence shows many peaks of active histone modification marks in all three cell types.
source: We found that it overlaps a DNase I-hypersensitive site (ENCODE Project Consortium, 2012) and shows many peaks of active histone modification marks in all three cell types (Figure 4c, Supplementary file 1f).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing histone modification data.

claim: The SATB2 sequence drives high expression in all three cell types (4th, 8th, and 19th percentile among active sequences, in ESCs, osteoblasts, and NPCs, respectively, FDR <10−5 across all).
source: Indeed, this sequence drives high expression in all three cell types (4th, 8th, and 19th percentile among active sequences, in ESCs, osteoblasts, and NPCs, respectively, FDR <10−5 across all).
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA experiment.

claim: The modern human SATB2 sequence is downregulating in all three cell types (−9% in ESCs, FDR = 6.8×10−4; −27% in osteoblasts, FDR = 2.2×10−42; −12% in NPCs, FDR = 1.1×10−7).
source: Although this sequence shows hallmarks of activity in modern humans, compared to the archaic sequence, the modern human sequence is downregulating in all three cell types (−9% in ESCs, FDR = 6.8×10−4, −27% in osteoblasts, FDR = 2.2×10−42, and −12% in NPCs, FDR = 1.1×10−7, Figure 4d).
evidence: This is a direct result from the MPRA experiment showing differential activity.

claim: SATB2 encodes a transcription factor expressed in developing bone and brain.
source: SATB2 encodes a TF expressed in developing bone and brain.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of SATB2.

claim: SATB2 activity promotes bone formation, jaw patterning, cortical upper layer neuron specification, and tumorigenesis.
source: Its activity promotes bone formation, jaw patterning, cortical upper layer neuron specification, and tumorigenesis (Zarate and Fish, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a known function of SATB2 and supported by a citation.

claim: Common variants near and within SATB2 are associated with brain and bone phenotypes including reaction time, anxiety, mathematical abilities, schizophrenia, autism, bone density, and facial morphology.
source: Genome-wide association studies show that common variants near and within SATB2 are mainly associated with brain and bone phenotypes, such as reaction time, anxiety, mathematical abilities, schizophrenia, autism, bone density, and facial morphology (Buniello et al., 2019; Claes et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as findings from GWAS studies and supported by citations.

claim: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SATB2 result in SATB2-associated syndrome, which primarily affects neurological and craniofacial phenotypes.
source: Heterozygous loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in SATB2 result in the SATB2-associated syndrome, which primarily affects neurological and craniofacial phenotypes.
evidence: This is stated as a known clinical syndrome associated with SATB2 mutations.

claim: SATB2-associated syndrome includes speech delay, behavioral anomalies, autistic tendencies, small jaws, dental abnormalities, and morphological changes to the palate.
source: This includes speech delay, behavioral anomalies (e.g., jovial personality, aggressive outbursts, and hyperactivity), autistic tendencies, small jaws, dental abnormalities, and morphological changes to the palate (Zarate et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as clinical features of SATB2-associated syndrome and supported by a citation.

claim: Reduced functional levels of SATB2 due to heterozygous LOF cause SATB2-associated syndrome phenotypes in both human and mouse.
source: Additionally, reduced functional levels of SATB2 due to heterozygous LOF have been shown to be the cause of these phenotypes in both human (Zarate and Fish, 2017; Zarate et al., 1993; Gigek et al., 2015; Qian et al., 2019) and mouse (Li et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019; Dobreva et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as findings from human and mouse studies and supported by multiple citations.

claim: 88% (15 out of 17) of SATB2-affected phenotypes are divergent between modern humans and Neanderthals.
source: From HPO, we generated a list of 17 phenotypes known to be affected by SATB2 and found that 88% (15) of them are divergent between these human groups (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a result from comparing SATB2-associated phenotypes to the fossil record.

claim: 80% (12 out of 15) of divergent SATB2-affected phenotypes match in direction between patients and the fossil record.
source: Yet, we observed a match in direction in 80% of the phenotypes (12 out of 15, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a result from comparing the direction of phenotypic changes.

claim: The observed number of SATB2 phenotypes that are both divergent and match in direction is 2.3-fold higher than expected by chance (p=1.3×10−4).
source: Overall, the observed number of phenotypes that are both divergent and match in their direction of change is 2.3-fold higher than expected by chance (p=1.3×10−4, hypergeometric test, Supplementary file 5, see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a statistical result showing enrichment of matching phenotypes.

claim: Changes to TF binding might have played a central role in shaping divergent modern human expression.
source: By comparing modern to archaic sequences, we investigated the regulatory potential of each of the 14,042 single-nucleotide variants that emerged and reached fixation or near fixation in modern humans. We found an association between divergent TF motifs and the sequences driving expression changes, suggesting that changes to TF binding might have played a central role in shaping divergent modern human expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the TF binding analysis results.

claim: Genes affecting the vocal tract and cerebellum might have been particularly affected by expression changes between modern and archaic humans.
source: Our results also suggest that genes affecting the vocal tract and cerebellum might have been particularly affected by these expression changes, which is in line with previous comparisons based on the fossil record (Neubauer et al., 2018; Gunz et al., 2019; Aiello and Dean, 2002; Kochiyama et al., 2018) and DNA methylation (Gokhman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the enrichment analysis results and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LentiMPRA library inserts were limited to ~200 bp in length due to oligonucleotide synthesis technical restrictions.
source: First, our lentiMPRA library inserts were limited to ~200 bp in length, due to oligonucleotide synthesis technical restrictions, which may be insufficient to detect the activity of longer enhancer sequences (Inoue et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a technical limitation of the study.

claim: Some minimally active sequences may not be expressed at a high enough level to pass the limit of detection.
source: Second, some minimally active sequences may not be expressed at a high enough level to pass our limit of detection.
evidence: This is stated as a potential limitation of the assay.

claim: Some sequences may regulate expression post-transcriptionally, which lentiMPRA is not designed to detect.
source: Third, some sequences may regulate expression post-transcriptionally, which lentiMPRA is not designed to detect.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the MPRA method.

claim: Transcriptional repression is less likely to be detected in lentiMPRA due to the low basal activity of the minimal promoter used.
source: Fifth, transcriptional repression is less likely to be detected due to the low basal activity of the mP used.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the experimental design.

claim: The proportion of active sequences observed in this study tends to be slightly lower than previous studies that pre-filtered for putative regulatory regions.
source: In line with the fact that our data was not pre-filtered for putative regulatory regions, the proportion of active sequences we observed tends to be slightly lower than these previous studies.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous MPRA studies.

claim: The magnitude of differential activity and the fraction of differentially active sequences out of active sequences were similar to previous studies.
source: However, the magnitude of differential activity, as well as the fraction of differentially active sequences out of the active sequences, was similar to previous studies (Weyer and Pääbo, 2016; Tewhey et al., 2016; Klein et al., 2018; Ryu et al., 2018; Uebbing et al., 2021; Mattioli et al., 2020; Prabhakar et al., 2008; Capra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous MPRA studies and supported by citations.

claim: Enhancers have been suggested to be an ideal substrate for evolution because of their tissue specificity and temporal modularity.
source: Enhancers have been suggested to be an ideal substrate for evolution because of their tissue specificity and temporal modularity (True and Carroll, 2002).
evidence: This is stated as an established principle in evolutionary biology and supported by a citation.

claim: Previous studies of introgression between archaic and modern humans suggested that enhancers are some of the most divergent regions between modern and archaic humans.
source: Indeed, previous studies of introgression between archaic and modern humans suggested that enhancers are some of the most divergent regions between modern and archaic humans (Petr et al., 2019; Silvert et al., 2019; Telis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: Brain-related putative enhancers show particularly low introgression, perhaps suggesting that the modern human sequences in these regions were adaptive.
source: In line with the enrichment we observed in NPCs, brain-related putative enhancers show particularly low introgression, perhaps suggesting that the modern human sequences in these regions were adaptive (Silvert et al., 2019; Telis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with a speculative interpretation, supported by citations.

claim: 53 of the 407 differentially active sequences were linked to genes which are known to affect one or more vocal tract phenotypes.
source: Overall, 53 of the 407 differentially active sequences were linked to genes which are known to affect one or more vocal tract phenotypes.
evidence: This is a result from linking differentially active sequences to genes and their associated phenotypes.

claim: The vocal tract went through particularly extensive regulatory changes between modern and archaic humans.
source: Previous reports have also suggested that the vocal tract went through particularly extensive regulatory changes between modern and archaic humans (Gokhman et al., 2020), as well as between humans and chimpanzees (Gokhman et al., 2021; Prescott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: The anatomy of the vocal tract differs between humans and chimpanzees and has been suggested to affect human phonetic range.
source: Intriguingly, the anatomy of the vocal tract differs between humans and chimpanzees and has been suggested to affect human phonetic range (Lieberman, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a known anatomical difference and its functional consequence, supported by a citation.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in motor control and perception, as well as more complex functions such as cognitive processing, emotional regulation, language, and working memory.
source: The cerebellum is involved in motor control and perception, as well as more complex functions such as cognitive processing, emotional regulation, language, and working memory (Mariën et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as known functions of the cerebellum and supported by a citation.

claim: The cerebellum has been described as the most morphologically divergent brain region between modern and archaic humans.
source: Interestingly, the cerebellum has been described as the most morphologically divergent brain region between modern and archaic humans (Neubauer et al., 2018; Kochiyama et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: Many introgressed sequences from Neanderthals were likely negatively selected, with the strongest effect in regulatory regions.
source: Studies of Neanderthal alleles introduced into modern humans through introgression provide a clue as to the functional effects of divergent loci between archaic and modern humans. These works have shown that many of the introgressed sequences were likely negatively selected, with the strongest effect in regulatory regions (Petr et al., 2019; Silvert et al., 2019), particularly in brain enhancers (Telis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies and supported by citations.

claim: The cerebellum is one of the regions with the most divergent expression between Neanderthal and modern human alleles.
source: Studies of introgressed sequences have also shown that the cerebellum is one of the regions with the most divergent expression between Neanderthal and modern human alleles (McCoy et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from a previous study and supported by a citation.

claim: This work provides a catalog providing regulatory insight into the sequence changes that separate modern from archaic humans.
source: Here, we present a catalog providing regulatory insight into the sequence changes that separate modern from archaic humans.
evidence: This is stated as the main contribution of the study.
